content.text:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Do not accept the initial offer as-is, but don’t walk away yet.**

It is a **good, market-competitive L6 offer**, but it is not sufficiently compelling for someone who:

- already makes approximately **$526,000**
- is happy at Meta
- was recruited rather than actively searching
- is taking switching, performance, team, and refresh-grant risk

On a four-year basis, the offer is only about **5% above your current annual compensation**, assuming no stock appreciation and no future grants at either company. That is too small a premium to justify an otherwise unnecessary move.

My recommendation:

> **Open by asking for $265,000 base, $1.4 million in initial RSUs, and a $200,000 sign-on bonus, while making clear that you are flexible on the mix.**

A counter around **$250,000–$260,000 base, $1.25–$1.35 million RSUs, and $100,000–$150,000 sign-on** would make the decision considerably more attractive.

---

## 1. What the offer is actually worth

First, confirm the vesting schedule in writing.

Google’s new-hire grants are commonly reported as front-loaded **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, although your individual grant agreement controls. Refresh grants are generally reported as vesting evenly rather than on the same front-loaded schedule. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

If your $1.08 million grant follows 38/32/20/10:

| Year | Base + target bonus | New-hire equity | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $282,000 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $282,000 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $282,000 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $282,000 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |
| **Four-year average** |  |  | **$552,000** |

This excludes:

- stock-price movement
- bonus over- or under-performance
- raises
- refresh grants
- promotions
- benefits differences

Your corresponding Meta numbers are:

- Current stated annual compensation: **$526,000**
- Next 12 months based on only $200,000 vesting: **$476,000**
- Four years at a constant $526,000: **$2.104 million**
- Google’s four-year offer value: **$2.208 million**
- Difference: **$104,000 over four years**, or **$26,000 per year**

So there are two different conclusions:

1. **Google is excellent in years one and two** because of front-loading.
2. **The guaranteed four-year economic improvement is modest**, and compensation falls sharply in years three and four unless refreshes materialize.

---

## 2. Is it a good L6 offer?

### Relative to Google’s market

Yes, broadly.

Recent self-reported data places Bay Area Google L6 Senior PM median compensation around **$551,000**, while another recent cut of U.S. data puts the L6 median around **$514,000** and the 90th percentile around **$671,000**. Your $552,000 four-year annualized offer is therefore approximately median—not a lowball, but not an exceptional package. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Your base is also essentially around the reported L6 median, although it is:

- **$5,000 below your Meta base**
- well below the **$271,000 top of the posted range**

Current Google Senior PM postings in San Francisco show similar broad base ranges plus a 20% bonus and equity, reinforcing that there is room above $235,000 within the level. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS))

### Relative to your personal alternative

It is not yet compelling.

Your relevant benchmark is not “average Google L6.” It is:

> “How much must Google pay to make a happy Meta IC6 voluntarily assume switching risk?”

A 5% four-year premium is generally not enough for that situation, particularly because:

- $200,000 of Meta equity will vest during the next 12 months
- you know your reputation and performance trajectory at Meta
- you do not yet know your manager, team dynamics, or performance trajectory at Google
- the later-year Google package depends heavily on discretionary refreshes
- a move resets your organizational capital and potentially your promotion clock

---

## 3. Don’t assign full value to refreshes

The recruiter was appropriately careful: refreshes exist, but the amount is not guaranteed. Google describes annual equity refresh decisions as depending on modeled recommendations using factors such as performance, location, and role, followed by manager discretion and higher-level review. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

You should therefore evaluate the offer in three ways:

1. **Zero-refresh case:** $552,000 four-year average.
2. **Conservative case:** assign perhaps 50% of whatever typical refresh the recruiter describes.
3. **Expected case:** model the actual timing and vesting of likely grants.

Do not simply add an alleged “typical annual refresh” to every year. A refresh awarded after you join will have its own vesting schedule, so only part of it may vest during your initial four years.

Ask the recruiter specifically:

- When would I first be eligible for a refresh?
- What was the modeled L6 PM refresh grant for someone meeting expectations in the most recent cycle?
- What are the 25th, median, and 75th percentile refreshes for L6 PMs in this location?
- Do refresh grants vest 25% per year?
- How is the first refresh prorated based on start date?
- Can you show me an illustrative vesting schedule including typical refreshes?

They may decline to provide numbers. That itself tells you not to count heavily on them.

---

## 4. What exactly to request

### Opening request

I would ask for:

- **Base: $265,000**
- **Initial RSUs: $1,400,000**
- **Sign-on: $200,000**

That is deliberately an opening position, not necessarily your minimum.

### Why these numbers are defensible

#### Base: $265,000

- It is within the posted $183,000–$271,000 range.
- You currently make $240,000.
- Google’s opening offer asks you to accept a base-pay reduction.
- You are an experienced Meta IC6 being recruited into a senior role.

Base may be the least flexible component, so be prepared for Google to move less here.

#### Equity: $1.4 million

Equity is the most important lever because:

- the current $1.08 million grant creates only a modest four-year premium
- the front-loaded schedule creates a significant year-four decline
- refreshes are uncertain
- you are giving up a known compensation trajectory at Meta

An ask of $1.4 million is a meaningful but not absurd increase: approximately 30% above the initial grant.

#### Sign-on: $200,000

Frame this as a **make-whole and transition payment** connected to your near-term Meta vesting and the risk of moving—not as an entitlement to both Google’s front-loaded equity and a dollar-for-dollar replacement.

Google may not agree that the entire $200,000 is a loss because its first-year equity is already heavily front-loaded. Still, asking for the full amount gives room to land at $100,000–$150,000.

If cash sign-on is constrained, offer alternatives:

- additional equity
- a split sign-on over years one and two
- a later start date after a meaningful Meta vest
- a guaranteed minimum first-year bonus, if available
- a combination of cash and GSUs

---

## 5. Your likely acceptable landing zone

Because you are happy at Meta, I would look for something around:

| Component | Initial offer | Reasonable landing zone |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $235,000 | **$250,000–$260,000** |
| Bonus | 20% | 20% |
| RSUs | $1.08M | **$1.25M–$1.35M** |
| Sign-on | $0 | **$100K–$150K** |

For example:

- $250,000 base
- $50,000 target bonus
- $1.25 million RSUs
- $100,000 sign-on

That equals:

- **$612,500 annualized recurring four-year value**, before refreshes
- **$637,500 four-year average including the sign-on**

That is roughly a **16% recurring premium** over your current $526,000 and begins to compensate you appropriately for moving risk.

I would not insist on every component individually. Optimize for total package value:

> “I’m flexible on the mix, but I need both the four-year economics and the near-term transition economics to improve.”

---

## 6. Suggested wording to the recruiter

You can say:

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and the role. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking and I’m happy at Meta, so the financial case needs to be meaningfully compelling for me to make a move.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526,000, and I have approximately $200,000 of Meta equity scheduled to vest over the next 12 months. On a four-year basis, the current Google offer annualizes to approximately $552,000 before uncertain refresh grants, so it represents only a modest premium over staying.
>
> A package that would make the decision much easier would be approximately $265,000 in base, $1.4 million in initial equity, and a $200,000 sign-on bonus. I understand there may be constraints on individual components, and I’m flexible on the mix, particularly between equity and sign-on. But I would need a materially stronger overall package to justify leaving a role where I’m happy and performing well.
>
> Could you take that back to compensation and see what flexibility exists?

Then stop talking. Do not immediately soften the request.

---

## 7. Also verify the level and role

Before deciding, ask:

- Was I evaluated only for L6, or was L7 considered?
- What specifically separated my interview performance from L7?
- What scope does this role own: one team, multiple teams, or a broader product area?
- What percentage of external L6 PM hires are promoted to L7, and on what typical timeline?
- Is this position tied to the current team, or could team matching change before the start date?
- What are the expectations during the first two performance cycles?

I would not make L7 a hard demand unless the role’s scope supports it, but it is worth understanding whether you are moving laterally, accepting narrower scope, or entering with a plausible L7 trajectory.

---

## Decision recommendation

### Accept if

- you prefer the role/team, **and**
- Google gets the package into roughly the **$600,000–$625,000+ recurring four-year annualized range**, or compensates for a lower recurring figure with a substantial sign-on.

### Consider accepting the existing offer only if

- you strongly prefer the Google role or manager
- you want to diversify away from Meta
- you expect to leave Google within two or three years, allowing you to capture the front-loaded years
- you have high confidence in meaningful refresh grants

### Stay at Meta if

- Google barely moves
- the recruiter relies mainly on unspecified future refreshes
- the role itself is not clearly better
- you expect to remain four-plus years
- compensation is your main criterion

**My actual call:** negotiate hard. If the final package remains close to **$235K / $47K / $1.08M / $0 sign-on**, I would stay at Meta. It is a respectable offer, but not enough of an upgrade for a happy, unsolicited candidate taking a discretionary-refresh and year-four compensation risk.

## My call: **lean accept**, assuming you like the role, manager, and scope

The revised offer is now financially compelling enough to justify the move. It isn’t an automatic yes regardless of the job, but **compensation is no longer a good reason to decline**.

### Four-year comparison

Ignoring raises, stock-price changes, refresh grants, and promotions at both companies:

| | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base over four years | $960K | $960K |
| Target bonus | $144K | $192K |
| Equity | $1.0M | $1.08M |
| Sign-on | — | $200K |
| **Four-year total** | **$2.104M** | **$2.432M** |
| **Annual average** | **$526K** | **$608K** |

Google is now approximately:

- **$328,000 ahead over four years**
- **$82,000 per year ahead on average**
- **15.6% above your current compensation** 

That is a reasonable switching premium for a lateral move.

## The important caveat

The $200,000 sign-on is one-time compensation. Excluding it, Google’s recurring four-year annualized package is:

- $240K base
- $48K target bonus
- $270K annualized equity
- **$558K total**

That is only **$32,000, or about 6%, above Meta’s $526K**. Therefore, the offer is especially attractive during the initial four-year grant period, but your longer-term compensation depends on:

- refresh grants
- raises
- promotion prospects
- stock performance
- whether you remain long enough to experience an equity cliff

Your four-year break-even point is simple: if you believe staying at Meta would average more than **$608,000 per year** over the next four years—perhaps because of promotion or strong refreshes—Meta could still be financially better.

## Don’t mentally treat the sign-on as merely canceling the Meta vest

It is understandable to say that Google is replacing the $200K you are leaving behind, but evaluate complete cash flows rather than labeling individual pieces.

In the next 12 months, you estimate Meta would pay approximately:

- $240K base
- $36K bonus
- $200K equity
- **$476K total**

At Google, assuming even equity vesting purely for illustration:

- $240K base
- $48K target bonus
- $270K equity
- $200K sign-on
- **$758K total**

That would put Google about **$282K ahead in year one**. If the new-hire grant is front-loaded, the first-year advantage would be larger. Verify the actual schedule in your offer documents. 

## Verify these terms before signing

You no longer need to negotiate the headline numbers, but obtain written clarification on:

1. **RSU vesting schedule**
   - Exact percentages by year
   - First vesting date
   - When the $1.08M is converted into a fixed number of shares

2. **Sign-on repayment**
   - Length of the clawback period
   - Whether repayment is prorated
   - Whether you repay the gross or net amount
   - Whether clawback applies after involuntary termination or only voluntary departure/termination for cause

3. **Bonus**
   - Whether your first-year bonus is prorated
   - Whether your start date affects eligibility
   - When it is paid

4. **Refresh eligibility**
   - When you first become eligible
   - Whether your start date could cause you to miss the first compensation cycle

5. **Start date**
   - Whether delaying your start until after an imminent Meta vest affects the sign-on or offer

That last point is worth asking carefully:

> “Is there any flexibility in start date to align with my current transition obligations, and would a later start date change any part of the package?”

Don’t explicitly demand both the $200K Meta vest and the full make-whole payment after representing that you would forfeit the vest. But if a normal transition date happens to let part of it vest, that is useful information.

## When I would still stay at Meta

I would decline despite the money if any of these are true:

- You have materially higher confidence in an upcoming Meta promotion or major refresh.
- The Google role has weaker scope, a questionable manager, or uncertain team placement.
- You would be moving mainly for money but already suspect you won’t enjoy the work.
- The sign-on has an unusually punitive or long clawback.
- You place a high value on your established reputation, influence, and job security at Meta.
- You expect to stay longer than four years but lack confidence that Google refreshes will support year-five compensation.

Organizational capital is real. Moving from a place where you are happy and established to an unknown environment should not be justified by a tiny premium. But **$328K of four-year incremental compensation is no longer tiny**.

## Recommendation

**If the Google role and manager are at least comparable to your current situation, accept.** The revised package clears a reasonable financial threshold for switching.

If the Google job itself appears meaningfully worse, stay at Meta—the offer is good, but it is not large enough to compensate for a role you expect to dislike.

I would not make another compensation counter after they have labeled this their best offer. Clarify the contractual details, make the role-based decision, and either accept cleanly or decline cleanly.
